Customer due diligence involves identifying the customer and verifying their identity using reliable, independent source documents, data or information. This includes obtaining information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship. Additionally, financial institutions should understand the ownership and control structure of the customer, particularly when dealing with legal persons and arrangements. The customer's beneficial owner(s) must also be identified and verified, with measures taken to prevent any natural person from exerting control through other means.

Customer due diligence (CDD) involves verifying the identity of customers and understanding the nature of their business relationships [1?]. 

It includes identifying the customer and verifying its identity using reliable, independent source documents, data, or information [1?]. 

This process also involves identifying the beneficial owner(s) of the customer and taking reasonable measures to verify their identity [2?]. 

Additionally, CDD requires understanding and, as appropriate, obtaining information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship [1?]. 

It also involves conducting ongoing due diligence on the business relationship and scrutiny of transactions undertaken throughout the course of that relationship [1?].

Domestic PEPs are individuals who are or have been entrusted domestically with prominent public functions, for example Heads of State or of government, senior politicians, senior government, judicial or military officials, senior executives of state-owned corporations, important political party officials [1].

The definition of PEPs is not intended to cover middle-ranking or more junior individuals in these categories [1].

The three lines of defence in operational risk are: business unit management, an independent corporate operational risk management function (CORF), and independent assurance.

Business unit management is the first line of defence, responsible for identifying and managing operational risks inherent in their respective business units [1?]. The second line of defence, the CORF, develops an independent view regarding business units' material operational risks, design and effectiveness of key controls, and risk tolerance [1]. The third line of defence provides independent assurance to the board of the appropriateness of the bank's operational risk management framework [1].

The three lines of defence in operational risk are business unit management, an independent corporate operational risk management function, and independent assurance.
Business unit management is the first line of defence and is responsible for identifying and managing operational risks inherent in their respective business units.
They are responsible for identifying and assessing the materiality of operational risks, and for reporting to senior management and the board of directors on the bank's risk exposures and capital positions [4?]. However, sound operational risk governance recognizes that business unit management is responsible for identifying and managing the risks inherent in the products, activities, processes and systems for which it is accountable.
The second line of defence is an independent corporate operational risk management function, also known as the second line of defence.
Its responsibilities include developing an independent view regarding business units' material operational risks, and challenging the relevance and consistency of the business unit's implementation of operational risk management tools and measurement activities.
This function should have a reporting structure independent of the risk-generating business units and be responsible for the design, maintenance and ongoing development of the operational risk management and measurement policies, standards and guidelines.
It also includes a Compliance function, and should ensure that each line of defence is adequately resourced, has clearly defined roles and responsibilities, and promotes a sound risk management culture across the organization.
The third line of defence provides independent assurance to the board of the appropriateness of the bank's operational risk management framework.
Its staff should not be involved in the development, implementation and operation of operational risk management processes by the other two lines of defence.
This function reviews generally are conducted by the bank's internal and/or external audit, but may also involve other suitably qualified independent third parties.

Independent assurance is the third line of defence, providing independent verification and validation of the operational risk management framework (ORMF) and ensuring that it is effective in managing operational risks.
